theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A ministry wants to expand after-school reading classes in rural St Thomas. A church network already runs classes there. Why might a partnering arrangement be the best approach?
options: It lets the ministry hand all responsibility for results to the churches
It means the ministry no longer has to report how the money is spent
Each side brings something the other lacks, towards a shared goal
It is the only way a ministry may spend money in a rural parish

questions.stem: In which situation is a partnering arrangement least suitable for a public body?
options: When another body has local knowledge and trust that the agency lacks
When several agencies each hold part of the funding a project needs
When a private firm has skills that would improve a public service
When the task is a legal duty only the body itself may perform

questions.stem: Two agencies share information about their programmes but plan and fund them separately. Where are they on the partnering continuum?
options: Full collaboration, with joint plans, budgets and shared decisions
Networking or coordinating, at the looser end
A joint venture, with a new legal body owned by both agencies
A merger, in which the two agencies have become one body

questions.stem: Before looking for partners, what should a parish municipal corporation do first?
options: Draft the partnership agreement so that partners can sign it quickly
Announce the partnership in the media to attract plenty of interest
Define the problem, the goals and what it needs from a partner
Choose a partner that the mayor already knows well and trusts

questions.stem: Two agencies want to record their shared aims and how they will cooperate, without creating legally binding money obligations. Which document usually fits?
options: A memorandum of understanding
A sale and purchase agreement
A competitive tender notice
A loan agreement with interest

questions.stem: When a public body pays a private firm to deliver a service to agreed standards, which arrangement is usually needed?
options: An informal exchange of emails between the two managers involved
A binding contract, awarded under the procurement rules
A memorandum of understanding with no duties on either side
A spoken agreement made at a meeting and noted in the minutes

questions.stem: What is a public-private partnership (PPP)?
options: A grant from the Government to a private firm with no conditions
The sale of a public body's assets to the highest private bidder
A loan from a private bank to a ministry to cover its payroll
A long-term deal in which a private firm shares a public project's risks

questions.stem: A ministry is about to partner with a non-governmental organisation (NGO) to run youth programmes. What is the main purpose of due diligence?
options: To check the NGO's legal status, finances, record and capacity
To agree the wording of the press release about the partnership
To decide which ministry staff will attend the launch ceremony
To compare how much the NGO pays its staff with other bodies

questions.stem: During due diligence, a ministry finds that a proposed partner has not filed its annual returns for three years. What should it do?
options: Ignore it, as paperwork does not affect what a partner delivers
Go ahead, but leave the finding out of the file to avoid delays
Raise it with the partner and weigh the risk before deciding
Publish the finding online at once to warn other public bodies

questions.stem: Three possible partners are scored on capacity (40% weight), experience (30%) and cost (30%). Partner A scores 8, 6 and 7; Partner B scores 6, 9 and 8; Partner C scores 9, 5 and 6. Which partner has the highest weighted score?
options: Partner A, with 7.1
Partner C, with 6.9
All three tie at 7.0
Partner B, with 7.5

questions.stem: Why should a public body use clear, published criteria when choosing a partner from several interested organisations?
options: So that it can choose a favoured partner without being questioned
So the choice is fair, open and can be justified if challenged
So that it need not check any partner's financial position
So that the unsuccessful organisations cannot ask for feedback

questions.stem: Which is the best statement of a shared objective for a partnership between a health agency and a community group?
options: Screen 2,000 adults in Clarendon for diabetes by March 2027
Work together closely to improve health in the community
Do as much screening as funds allow over the coming year
Make the partnership a real success for both partners

questions.stem: Why must a partnership agreement set out each partner's roles and responsibilities clearly?
options: So that each partner can refuse any extra work that comes up
So the larger partner can change the roles whenever it likes
So tasks are not missed or doubled and each can be held to account
So the agreement can be kept short and never needs reviewing

questions.stem: A J$24,000,000 project is shared: the agency pays 40%, a private firm 45% and an NGO 15%. How much does the private firm contribute?
As its in-kind contribution, an NGO will provide four staff for six months. Each person's time is valued at J$150,000 a month. What is the value of this contribution?
In a partnership agreement, what should the governance section set out?
options: The logo and colours to be used on all partnership materials
The salaries of the staff employed by each of the partners
Who decides what, how, and how often the partners meet
The history of each partner organisation since it began

questions.stem: In a partnership to build and run a market in Half Way Tree, how should the risks be shared?
options: Each risk goes to the partner best able to manage it
All risks stay with the public body, as it is the larger
All risks pass to the private partner, as it makes a profit
Risks are split equally, whatever their nature or size

questions.stem: A university and a ministry will jointly develop a training app for farmers. What should their agreement say about the app?
options: Nothing, since such questions can be settled after the launch
Who owns it, who may use it, and how farmers' data is protected
That the university's students may sell the app as their own
That ministry IT staff may change it without asking anyone

questions.stem: Why should a partnership agreement include a dispute resolution clause?
options: So that any partner may walk away at once if it disagrees with the rest
So that every disagreement goes straight to the courts for a ruling
So that the larger partner always has the final word
So disputes are settled in agreed steps, such as talks then mediation

questions.stem: What should the exit section of a partnering agreement cover?
options: How and when partners may leave, and what happens to assets
Where the emergency exits are in each partner's offices
Which staff will leave their jobs when the work has ended
The farewell event to be held when the partnership is complete

questions.stem: Before a ministry's director signs a partnering agreement with a private firm, what should happen?
options: The firm's lawyer should approve it on behalf of both sides
The director should sign at once to avoid losing the partner
The ministry's legal officers review it and approvals are obtained
The agreement should be posted online for public comment first

questions.stem: A partner asks an agency's project officer to sign a co-funding agreement worth J$15,000,000. Her written authority lets her sign up to J$2,000,000. What should she do?
options: Sign it, since the partner needs the agreement urgently
Sign it, then tell her manager about it the following week
Split it into several small agreements and sign each one
Refer it to the officer with authority for that amount

questions.stem: Which practice does most to build trust between partners early in a partnership?
options: Keeping problems hidden so the other partner does not worry
Sharing information openly and doing what was promised
Letting the partner with more money make every decision
Meeting only once a problem has become serious enough

questions.stem: A large ministry is partnering with a small community group in Trench Town. What should the ministry do to make the partnership work well?
options: Make all the decisions, since it provides most of the funds
Use only its own reporting forms, however long they may be
Respect the group's knowledge and give it a real say
Expect the group to adopt every one of the ministry's procedures

questions.stem: How should partners know whether their partnership is achieving its goals?
options: Agree measures and targets at the start and review them together
Each partner judges success in its own way, in private
Wait until the agreement ends before looking at results
Count the number of meetings the partners have held

questions.stem: Apart from results, what does a partnership "health check" look at?
options: The physical health of the staff in each partner organisation
The cleanliness of the offices where the partners hold meetings
The number of public complaints made about each partner
How well partners communicate, trust and work together

questions.stem: A partner's quarterly report shows it is behind on its agreed targets. What should the agency's partnership manager do first?
options: End the agreement at once and look for a new partner
Meet the partner to find the causes and agree a recovery plan
Tell the media that the partner has failed to deliver
Hold back all payments without telling the partner why

questions.stem: A private firm offers to fund a ministry's school nutrition programme if its sugary drink brand appears on all the materials. What is the main concern?
options: The firm may not have enough money to fund the programme
The programme would have too many partners to manage well
The branding would clash with the programme's health aims
The ministry would have to print the materials in more colours

questions.stem: An officer helping to choose a partner for a housing project is a director of one of the bidding companies. What must happen?
options: He declares the interest and takes no part in the decision
He takes part but gives that company slightly lower marks
He resigns as a director after the contract is signed
He keeps it private, since he does not own any shares

questions.stem: Why do partners agree a communications protocol for a joint programme?
options: So that only one partner is ever named in the media coverage
So messages, branding and credit are agreed and consistent
So that partners never need to talk to each other directly
So that the public cannot contact any partner with questions

questions.stem: A ministry can deliver a training programme itself for J$18,000,000, or through a partnership that costs it J$12,000,000 for the same results. What does this suggest?
options: The ministry should deliver it itself, as cost does not matter
The partnership saves J$30,000,000 for the same results
The two options cost the same once staff time is ignored
The partnership may give better value, if risks are managed

questions.stem: A ministry passes J$5,000,000 to a partner NGO for a programme. Who remains accountable for showing how the public money was used?
options: Only the NGO, once the money has left the ministry
No one, since the money was a gift to the community
The ministry, which must require reports and checks
The Auditor General alone, without the ministry's help

questions.stem: What is the main job of the partnership manager (liaison officer) that each partner appoints?
options: To be the daily contact and keep the joint work on track
To approve all of the other partner's spending without review
To represent the partnership in court if a dispute arises
To write every partner's reports without any of their input

questions.stem: A three-year partnering agreement is about to end. What should the partners do before deciding whether to renew it?
options: Renew it automatically, since partnerships always get better
End it automatically, since all partnerships should be short
Ask only the junior staff whether they enjoyed the partnership
Review results, costs and the relationship against the aims

questions.stem: A ministry and a private firm keep clashing because the firm decides quickly while the ministry needs several approvals. What is the best way forward?
options: The firm should leave, since the two cultures cannot mix
Agree realistic timelines and explain the approvals early
The ministry should skip its approvals to match the firm
The firm should be told to stop asking about decisions

questions.stem: Why should a municipal corporation involve local residents when developing a partnership to manage a community park?
options: Residents can shape the plans and help the park succeed
Residents must approve every payment the partners make
It allows the council to pass all the costs to residents
The law requires every resident to sign the agreement

questions.stem: Two agencies will share records of the clients they both serve. Which step fits the general purpose of the data protection law?
options: Share all records freely, as both are government bodies
Let any officer in either agency see all shared records
Agree what data is shared, why, and how it is kept secure
Email the records as open spreadsheets to save time

questions.stem: A donor-funded partnership will end in two years. What should the partners plan now so that the benefits last?
options: Ask the donor to keep funding the programme for ever
How the work will be funded and run after the donor leaves
A closing ceremony to mark the end of the partnership
Stopping all activities a year before the funds run out

questions.stem: While a partnering agreement is being negotiated, a private partner asks for exclusive rights to all future projects in the parish. How should the agency respond?
options: Agree, as exclusive rights will make the partner work harder
Agree, but only for the next ten years of projects
Refuse to discuss any other terms with the partner
Decline, as it would limit fair competition and value

questions.stem: Midway through a partnership, both partners want to change the delivery dates. What should they do?
options: Change the dates by phone and carry on as before
Let each partner keep to its own new dates as it wishes
Agree the change in writing, as the agreement allows
End the agreement and start a new one from scratch

questions.stem: Why should a public body record the lessons learned at the end of a partnership?
options: So future partnerships avoid problems and repeat successes
So that staff can be blamed for problems in the partnership
So the partner cannot work with other public bodies again
So that the body need not review any future partnerships

questions.stem: Which is NOT usually included in a partnering agreement?
options: The partners' contributions and responsibilities
The home addresses of each partner's staff
How disputes between the partners will be settled
How and when the agreement will be reviewed

questions.stem: One agency will provide payroll processing to another agency for a fee, with set turnaround times and quality standards. Which document best sets this out?
options: A memorandum of understanding
A joint press statement
A letter of thanks
A service level agreement

questions.stem: The partnership managers from two agencies cannot agree how to share a cost overrun. Under a well-drafted agreement, what usually happens next?
options: The matter goes to the partners' senior officers to settle
The partner with the larger budget decides on its own
The partnership ends automatically on that same day
Both managers are removed from the partnership at once

questions.stem: Why should partners report their joint achievements to stakeholders, giving fair credit to each partner?
options: So the public body can claim all of the success as its own
So that partners compete for the most credit in the media
It builds goodwill, supports funding and keeps partners committed
It removes the need for formal reports to the funders

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term describes a partner's contribution of staff time, premises or equipment instead of cash?
What document records that parties intend to make an agreement, before the full agreement is drafted?
What three-word term describes getting the best mix of cost, quality and results from public funds?
What term describes a new business entity owned jointly by two or more partners for a specific purpose?
What name is usually given to the group of senior people from each partner that oversees a partnership and makes its key decisions?
What term describes a process in which a neutral third person helps partners in dispute to reach their own agreement?
What word describes the extra value created when partners achieve more together than they could separately?
A possible partner scores 7 on quality, which has a 60% weight, and 9 on cost, which has a 40% weight. What is its weighted score?
An agency contributes J$6,000,000 to a J$20,000,000 partnership project. What percentage of the cost is this?
A partner has reached 1,440 households against its target of 1,800. What percentage of the target is this?
What one word describes being answerable for how public money and decisions are used?
What term describes funding where each partner puts in money in an agreed ratio, for example a donor matching the agency's contribution?
What word describes the people a partnership's programme is meant to help?
What term is used for a clause that excuses partners from their duties when events beyond their control, such as a hurricane, stop the work?
What one word names the agreed length of time for which a partnering agreement lasts?

essays.stem: Your agency wants to work with private firms and NGOs to provide skills training for young people in the western parishes. Plan the steps you would take to develop the partnering arrangement, from scoping to signing.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin by scoping: defining the problem, such as high youth unemployment in Westmoreland and Hanover, setting measurable goals, for example 1,200 young people trained and 60% placed in jobs within two years, and listing what the agency can offer and what it needs from partners, such as workplaces, trainers and community links. I would check the agency's mandate, budget and the rules that apply, including the procurement rules if services are to be bought. I would map possible partners and consult stakeholders, including young people. Next I would set clear selection criteria with weights, invite expressions of interest openly, score the responses fairly and carry out due diligence on the shortlisted partners. I would then negotiate the terms: objectives, each partner's contributions and roles, governance, reporting, risk sharing, data protection, branding, dispute resolution, review and exit. The draft would be reviewed by our legal officers and approved by those with the authority to sign. Finally, I would plan the launch, the first steering committee meeting and the monitoring system.
markingPoints: Scopes the need, measurable goals and what partners must bring
Checks mandate, budget and the rules that apply
Selects partners fairly with criteria and due diligence
Negotiates the main terms of the agreement
Obtains legal review and proper approvals, and plans governance and monitoring

essays.stem: Compare a memorandum of understanding, a contract and a public-private partnership as partnering arrangements, and recommend which suits a ministry that will give J$8,000,000 to an NGO to run a youth mentoring programme.
essays.modelAnswer: A memorandum of understanding records shared aims and how partners will cooperate. It is quick to agree and flexible, but it is usually not legally binding, so it gives little protection where money and firm commitments are involved. A contract is legally binding: it sets out what each party must deliver, payment terms, standards, reporting and remedies if things go wrong. It takes longer to draft and is less flexible, but it protects public funds. Where the ministry is buying a service, the procurement rules apply. A public-private partnership is a long-term arrangement, often for infrastructure, in which a private partner invests and shares significant risks; it is complex, slow to set up and suited to large projects, not a small social programme. For a ministry giving J$8,000,000 to an NGO, I would recommend a binding grant or service agreement in contract form, because public money must be accounted for. It should set targets, payment in stages linked to results, reporting, audit rights and exit terms. An MOU could sit alongside it to describe the wider cooperation.
markingPoints: Describes the MOU accurately, with a strength and a limit
Describes the contract accurately, with a strength and a limit
Describes the PPP accurately and its usual use
Recommends a binding agreement for the funded programme
Justifies it by accountability for public funds and names key terms

essays.stem: Two NGOs want to partner with a municipal corporation. Criteria and weights are capacity 50%, experience 30% and community links 20%. NGO X scores 7, 8 and 9; NGO Y scores 9, 7 and 6. Work out each weighted score and explain how the council should make its final choice.
essays.modelAnswer: NGO X: 7 x 0.5 = 3.5, 8 x 0.3 = 2.4 and 9 x 0.2 = 1.8, a total of 7.7. NGO Y: 9 x 0.5 = 4.5, 7 x 0.3 = 2.1 and 6 x 0.2 = 1.2, a total of 7.8. NGO Y is ahead, but only by 0.1, which is too small to decide the matter on its own, since scores involve judgement. The council should first check that the scoring was done fairly by more than one person, with no conflicts of interest, and that the weights were set before the bids were opened. It should then rely on due diligence: checking each NGO's legal registration, audited accounts, past results, references and whether it has the staff to deliver. It might interview both NGOs. It should also consider risk: Y has more capacity but weaker community links, which might make it harder to reach residents, while X is well rooted locally but may need support to grow. The council should record its reasons clearly, choose the partner that gives the best overall value and lowest risk, and give feedback to the unsuccessful NGO.
markingPoints: Calculates X correctly as 7.7
Calculates Y correctly as 7.8
Recognises that a small gap should not decide alone and checks the fairness of scoring
Uses due diligence, references or interviews and weighs risks
Records reasons and gives feedback

essays.stem: Describe the main sections of a partnering agreement between a public body and a private firm, and explain why each is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: The agreement should begin with the parties and the purpose, so it is clear who is bound and why the partnership exists. The objectives and expected results, with measurable targets, set what success means. The roles and responsibilities section says who does what, so nothing is missed or doubled. The contributions section lists each partner's cash and in-kind inputs and payment terms, protecting public funds. Governance sets out the steering committee, partnership managers, meeting schedule and who decides what. Reporting and monitoring explain what reports are due, when, and the right to audit. Risk sharing says who carries each risk, including insurance and force majeure. Intellectual property, data protection and confidentiality clauses protect ownership and personal data in line with the law. A communications clause agrees branding and publicity. The dispute resolution clause sets steps, such as talks between managers, then senior officers, then mediation. Finally, the term, review, variation and exit clauses say how long it lasts, how it can be changed in writing and how a partner may leave, with assets and records handled fairly.
markingPoints: Includes parties, purpose and measurable objectives
Includes roles and contributions, with reasons
Includes governance, reporting and audit, with reasons
Includes risk, IP, data protection and communications clauses
Includes dispute resolution, term, variation and exit, with reasons

essays.stem: A municipal corporation plans to partner with a private firm to rebuild and run a public market for 15 years. Evaluate the main risks and explain how the corporation should manage them.
essays.modelAnswer: Construction risk is the danger that the market is late or over budget; it is best carried by the firm, through fixed-price terms and penalties for delay. Demand risk is that fewer vendors or shoppers use the market than forecast, cutting income; this may need to be shared, with realistic forecasts and a review clause. Affordability is a social risk: higher stall fees could push out small vendors, so the agreement should cap fee increases and protect existing vendors. Performance risk covers poor cleaning, security or maintenance over 15 years, which needs clear service standards, regular inspections and the right to deduct payments. Financial risk is that the firm fails; due diligence, guarantees and step-in rights reduce it. Natural hazards such as hurricanes need insurance and a force majeure clause. Reputational and political risks arise if the public sees the deal as unfair, so the process must follow the procurement rules and be transparent. Overall, the partnership can work if each risk goes to the partner best able to manage it and the corporation keeps strong monitoring.
markingPoints: Identifies construction, demand and performance risks
Identifies social (affordability), financial and natural hazard risks
Allocates each risk to the partner best able to manage it
Proposes controls such as standards, inspections, insurance and step-in rights
Considers transparency and reaches an overall judgement

essays.stem: Describe the governance and monitoring arrangements you would set up for a partnership between a ministry, a private firm and two NGOs delivering a community health programme.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up a steering committee with one senior member from each partner, chaired by the ministry, meeting each quarter to set direction, approve plans and budgets, review progress and settle issues that managers cannot. Each partner would appoint a partnership manager as the daily contact; these managers would meet monthly as a working group to coordinate activities and solve problems. The agreement would set out who decides what, so decisions are not delayed. For monitoring, the partners would agree a results framework at the start, with baselines and targets, for example the number of people screened, referrals completed and follow-up rates. Each partner would submit a short monthly activity report and a quarterly report against targets and spending, using a shared template. The ministry would make spot checks and could arrange an audit, as public money is involved. Once a year the committee would hold a partnership health check on communication, trust and how well the partners work together, as well as results. Risks and issues would be kept in a shared register, and lessons recorded.
markingPoints: Sets up a steering committee with a clear role and schedule
Appoints partnership managers and a working group
Agrees a results framework with baselines and targets
Sets reporting, spot checks and audit rights
Includes a health check of the relationship and a risk register

essays.stem: A large government agency is developing a partnership with a small community-based organisation in an inner-city area. Explain how the agency should build a strong, fair relationship.
essays.modelAnswer: The agency should recognise that the community organisation brings things it lacks: trust, local knowledge and the ability to reach residents. It should treat the organisation as a partner, not a contractor, involving it in planning from the start and giving it a real voice in decisions through the steering group. Because there is an imbalance of size and money, the agency should avoid imposing heavy procedures; reporting forms should be simple and proportionate. It may need to help build the organisation's capacity, for example by training in financial records or paying part of its running costs, so that it can meet accountability requirements. Payments should be made on time, since small organisations cannot cover delays. Communication should be regular and open, with named contacts on both sides, and the agency should keep its promises. The agreement should be written in plain language and explained. Credit for results should be shared publicly. Finally, the agency should ask for the organisation's feedback on the relationship and act on it.
markingPoints: Recognises what the community organisation brings
Involves it in planning and decisions
Keeps procedures proportionate and helps build capacity
Pays on time and communicates openly, keeping promises
Shares credit and seeks feedback on the relationship

essays.stem: Explain how a public body stays accountable for public money it passes to partners, and the controls it should build into a partnering arrangement.
essays.modelAnswer: When a public body passes money to a partner, it does not pass on its accountability. It must still be able to show Parliament, auditors and the public that the money was used for the agreed purpose, with good value and without fraud. To do this, it should choose partners through a fair, recorded process, with due diligence on their finances and governance, and with conflicts of interest declared. The agreement should set clear objectives, a budget and eligible costs. Money should be released in stages, linked to agreed results and reports, rather than all at once. Partners should keep proper records and receipts, submit regular financial and progress reports, and give the body the right to inspect records and to arrange audits. The body's officers should check reports, make site visits and follow up any concerns quickly. The agreement should allow the body to hold back or recover money if it is misused, and to end the partnership. All decisions, approvals and checks should be documented, and results reported publicly where appropriate.
markingPoints: States that accountability stays with the public body
Uses fair selection and due diligence, with conflicts declared
Releases money in stages linked to results and reports
Includes record keeping, inspection and audit rights, and site checks
Allows recovery or termination and documents decisions

essays.stem: Six months into a partnership, a private partner is behind its targets, reports arrive late and meetings have become tense. Explain how you, as the agency's partnership manager, would handle the situation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by getting the facts: the targets and actual results, the dates reports were due and received, and the notes of recent meetings, so the discussion is based on evidence. I would also ask my own team whether the agency has contributed to the problem, for example through late payments, slow approvals or unclear instructions. I would then meet the partner's manager privately, explain my concerns calmly, and listen to their view of the causes, which might include staff shortages, unclear targets or tension with our officers. Together we would agree a recovery plan with specific actions, owners and dates, and any support the agency can give. We might adjust the reporting dates or template if they are unrealistic, provided the change is agreed in writing. I would arrange more frequent check-ins until things improve and keep a record of what is agreed. If problems continue, I would follow the escalation steps in the agreement: first to senior officers, then the steering committee, and, if needed, mediation. Ending the partnership would be a last resort.
markingPoints: Gathers facts and checks the agency's own part in the problem
Meets the partner calmly and listens to the causes
Agrees a recovery plan with actions, owners, dates and support
Increases monitoring and records agreements, varying terms in writing if needed
Uses the agreed escalation steps, with termination as a last resort

essays.stem: A three-year training partnership cost the agency J$45,000,000 and trained 2,700 people against a target of 3,000. The agency's own training costs J$20,000 per person. Evaluate the partnership and recommend whether to renew it.
essays.modelAnswer: The partnership trained 2,700 people, which is 90% of the target of 3,000. The cost per person trained was J$45,000,000 divided by 2,700, about J$16,667, which is lower than the agency's own cost of J$20,000 per person. Training the same 2,700 people in-house would have cost J$54,000,000, so the partnership saved about J$9,000,000. On cost and volume, the partnership looks like good value, although it fell 10% short of its target. However, I would want more information before deciding: the quality of the training, the share of trainees who passed and found jobs, feedback from trainees and employers, and whether the partners worked well together. I would also find out why the target was missed. If quality and job results are at least as good as the agency's own, I would recommend renewing the partnership, with a revised agreement that addresses the causes of the shortfall, sets outcome targets such as job placements, and links part of the payments to results.
markingPoints: Calculates 90% of target correctly
Calculates the cost per person (about J$16,667) and compares it with J$20,000
Notes the saving against in-house delivery (about J$9,000,000)
Identifies further information needed (quality, outcomes, relationship, cause of shortfall)
Makes a justified recommendation with improved terms

practical1.title: Scope a partnership and recommend a partner
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a public body (for example a parish municipal corporation) wants a partner to run a youth skills programme, and three organisations have sent short proposals. The pack includes each organisation's profile, simple accounts and references. As a group, prepare a scoping paper and a partner recommendation. Each member has a named role: scoping lead (writes a one-page scoping paper: the need, measurable goals, what the body offers and what it needs from a partner); criteria lead (sets the selection criteria and weights before the proposals are opened, and records that this was done first); scoring analyst (builds a weighted scoring sheet in a spreadsheet, enters each member's scores and works out the totals, checking every figure twice); due diligence officer (completes a due diligence checklist for each organisation and notes any red flags); and recommendation writer (writes a one-page memo recommending a partner, with reasons, risks and next steps). In a group of four, the scoping lead also sets the criteria. Every member scores the proposals separately before the scores are combined, and every member presents part of the recommendation to the assessor.
materials: Case pack and three proposals from the assessor
Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Due diligence checklist and memo templates
photos: The criteria and weights, dated before the proposals were opened
The weighted scoring spreadsheet on screen with each member's scores
The completed due diligence checklists with red flags marked
The recommendation memo and the group presenting it
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Goals in the scoping paper are clear and measurable
Criteria and weights were set before the proposals were scored
Weighted scores are calculated correctly and were checked twice
Due diligence covers legal status, finances, record, capacity and conflicts of interest
The recommendation is justified by the scores and the due diligence, and names the risks
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the proposals and accounts as confidential; return all papers to the assessor
Declare any personal link to a made-up organisation's details, as you would in real work
Respect each other's scores and views, and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Negotiate and draft a partnering agreement
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a ministry and a private company (or an NGO) have agreed in principle to run a joint programme, such as a school breakfast scheme in two parishes, and must now agree the terms. Part A (45 minutes): the group splits into two sides, each with a confidential brief from the assessor. Ministry side: a lead negotiator and a legal and finance adviser who checks costs, contributions and risks. Partner side: a lead negotiator and a programme manager. The fifth member is the facilitator and recorder, who keeps time and records what is agreed; in a group of four, the ministry adviser also records. Part B (45 minutes): negotiate the key terms: objectives and targets, contributions in cash and in kind (in J$), roles, governance, reporting, branding, data protection, risk sharing, dispute resolution, review and exit. Part C (1 hour): together, draft the heads of the partnering agreement (two to three pages), a governance chart showing the steering committee and partnership managers, and a risk table with at least five risks and who carries each. Each member drafts at least one section, and the two lead negotiators sign the heads of agreement.
materials: Case card and confidential side briefs from the assessor
Agreement, governance chart and risk table templates
Computer and printer, or flipchart paper and markers
A table set up for the negotiation
photos: The negotiation in progress (faces only if all agree)
The recorder's list of agreed and open terms
The drafted heads of agreement with signatures
The governance chart and the risk table
checklist: Prepared using the side brief and kept within its limits
Negotiated respectfully, looking for shared interests
Agreed objectives are measurable and contributions add up correctly
The draft covers roles, governance, reporting, data protection, disputes, review and exit
Risks are given to the partner best able to manage them
Drafted a clear, accurate section of the agreement
The governance chart shows who decides what and how often they meet
safety: Keep each side's brief private until the negotiation ends, then return all papers to the assessor
Use only the made-up case; do not discuss real organisations' confidential matters
Keep the negotiation respectful: challenge positions, not people
Share the drafting fairly and take a short break between parts
